title: 6 Fighter Jets That Can Pull The Most Gs - SlashGear
content: Modern fighter jets are among the most complex and impressive pieces of military machinery ever put into service. They're capable of reaching incredible speeds, and thanks to advancements like thrust vectoring, they're far more maneuverable than ever before. Flying one takes a great deal of training and skill to not only pull off high-speed maneuvers, but also to stay conscious due to the high G-forces a pilot experiences while flying a fighter jet. G-force is the measure of gravity endured by a pilot during flight. 1G is what everyone experiences on Earth — it's the baseline gravity we're all accustomed to. Fighter jets changing direction quickly increase the number of Gs felt by the pilot, and the higher they get, the more dangerous it becomes. Modern G-suits are pressurized to limit this danger, so while most people could remain conscious at around 5Gs, something you might experience on a roller coaster, fighter pilots typically endure up to 9Gs. When it comes to measuring the Gs a fighter jet can pull, the concern isn't the pilot's safety, but rather a measurement of the structural capability of the aircraft. Most can pull up to 9Gs, but some are rated higher, despite the risk to the pilot. In rare cases, fighter jets have pushed to around 12Gs in emergency situations, and some pilots have proven that they can endure this for short periods. These aircraft can pull more Gs than other modern fighter jets. The United States military's second fifth-generation fighter began operating in 2015, and the F-35 Lightning II comes in three variants. The F-35A belongs to the U.S. Air Force (USAF), the F-35B is capable of vertical take-off and landing and is flown by the U.S. Marine Corps, and the F-35C is a carrier-based version used by the U.S. Navy. While the B and C variants are rated at 7G and 7.5G, respectively, the F-35A has a maximum G-limit of +9Gs, making it the strongest F-35 model. The F-35A runs on an exceptionally powerful engine, the Pratt & Whitney F135-PW-100, which produces 40,000 pounds of thrust. This gives the F-35A the power it needs to reach speeds of Mach 1.6 (1,228 mph), and it's also highly maneuverable, thanks to its impressive flight control software. This helps control the aircraft during different types of flight operations, including high alpha maneuvers, which is when an aircraft like the F-35A uses an incredibly high angle of attack. While pilots can fly up to 9Gs, which is the limit of the F-35A, there have been instances of pilots experiencing oxygen deprivation (hypoxia) during flights. In 2017, Luke Air Force Base, Arizona, grounded 55 F-35s for 11 days following pilot reports of hypoxia. Steps were taken to limit the problem while the USAF investigated the cause. Eventually, flight operations returned to normal after the USAF addressed the oxygen generation system and other elements, enabling a return to normal flight operations. The F-22 Raptor is the world's first fifth-generation fighter jet, and it remains one of the most advanced aircraft operating today. It was so expensive to develop that fewer than 200 aircraft were initially produced. As of this writing, it's unlikely that any additional F-22s will be made and put into service. That makes flying it a rare opportunity for any USAF fighter pilot. In terms of speed, the F-22 Raptor is fast. Its supercruise ability enables supersonic cruising speeds up to Mach 1.5 (1,151 mph) without the need for its afterburner, and because the F-22 features 2D thrust vectoring, it's exceptionally maneuverable. The F-22 is rated with a +9/-3 G-limit, where +9 refers to upward G-forces, and -3 is for its downward G-force limit. Those figures are the extremes of what a human can endure while operating a fighter jet, even with G-suits and extensive training in centrifuges. Interestingly, several pilots have nearly blacked out while flying the F-22, but not because of the intense G-forces sustained during operation. In July 2012, the Pentagon reported at least 11 incidents of pilots becoming woozy and nearly blacking out. The subsequent investigation determined the G-forces weren't the cause, but rather the G-suits were. Due to a faulty valve, the suits would inflate their air-filled bladders prematurely. This made it difficult to breathe, resulting in hypoxia, but fortunately the problem was addressed. It's not just American aircraft that endure high Gs; the Russian Federation's Sukhoi Su-57 "Felon" is also rated up to 9Gs. Introduced in 2020 as the first Russian-designed fighter jet with stealth capabilities, this multirole fighter boasts plenty of impressive stats and equipment. It's not only stealth capable, it also features supercruise, supermaneuvrability, and more, aligning closely with the F-22 Raptor and F-35 Lightning II's flight capabilities. Since its introduction, Russia has continuously produced Su-57s to meet its goal of 76 aircraft by 2027. Apparently, it's well on its way to reaching that goal, though the Su-57 has seen only limited combat, as Russia prefers to keep it safe from Ukrainian air defenses during the Russia-Ukraine war. While the Su-57 is undeniably fast, its high G-limit threshold comes into play via its supermaneuvrability, which is achieved via its 3D thrust-vectoring engine nozzles, digital fly-by-wire system, and its aerodynamic design. The Su-57's 3D thrust vectoring exceeds the F-22's capabilities, as it affects not just the pitch, but also the yaw and roll. While there aren't any public records of pilots blacking out while flying the Su-57, there have been accidents. An Su-57 used for training crashed in July 2026, though Russia claimed this was due to a technical malfunction. Regardless, Russia, like the U.S. and other nations, employs high-tech G-suits to ensure their pilots maintain consciousness while flying advanced fighter jets. Russia began testing a new G-suit specifically designed for the Su-57 in 2019, showing an increased interest in pilot safety. France developed the Dassault Rafale as its primary fourth-generation multirole fighter, which entered service in 2001. The Rafale is one of the most innovative fighters of its generation, thanks to its use of a digital fly-by-wire system. Along with the aircraft's canards, this gives the Rafale improved aerodynamics and maneuverability. It's powered by two Snecma M88 turbofan engines and is capable of reaching Mach 1.8 (1,381 mph), so the Rafale is undoubtedly fast. In fact, a Rafale successfully "downed" an F-22 Raptor in an exercise in 2009, showing that it had what it takes to go up against a higher-generation fighter. The Rafale is rated up to +9Gs and -3.2Gs, making it one of the strongest European fighter jets in active service. However, in emergency situations, the Rafale has demonstrated a capability of +11Gs. While that wouldn't be survivable for long, pilots have remained conscious at and above 11Gs for short durations. While the aircraft can handle that many Gs, normal operations are limited to the standard scale, and higher than 9Gs are only reached during emergencies. There aren't any known instances of pilots passing out while flying a Rafale, but there have been accidents. In December 2007, a Rafale crashed in southwestern France. The investigation found that the pilot became disoriented, though it wasn't made public whether that disorientation was the result of hypoxia. France uses its own domestic G-suits designed by Safran, which outfit all French pilots operating the Rafale and similar aircraft. Another European fighter jet from the fourth generation featuring canards, Sweden's greatest fighter jet, the Saab JAS 39 Gripen entered service in 1997, preceding the Dassault Rafale by several years. Despite this, it's an incredibly advanced fourth-generation fighter jet that features improved fly-by-wire flight controls to aid in its maneuverability. The Gripen is also fast, thanks to its single General Electric F414, which is the engine installed on the most recent variants. It's also the same engine used in the F/A-18 Super Hornet, so it's been in use for some time on several aircraft. The engine provides enough power to give the Gripen a top speed of Mach 2 (1,535 mph), and thanks to its overall design, the aircraft features excellent maneuverability. It is rated for +9Gs and -3Gs, but like the Dassault Rafale, it can exceed this during emergency situations. The maximum possible G-limit of the Gripen is 12Gs, which is incredibly high. At time of writing, there are no reported incidents of Gripen pilots blacking out during flights, though there have been accidents. These are largely attributed to technical and mechanical failures, so despite the possibility of hitting 12Gs, it appears that pilots have safely flown the Gripen for decades. This is likely due to the use of an advanced Swedish G-suit worn by all pilots during operation. Granted, other nations operate the Gripen, but for Sweden, high Gs and well-made G-suits keep pilots safely flying the impressive fourth-generation fighter. While the U.S. began flying the F-15 Eagle back in 1976, the variant currently flying is a vastly improved, modernized aircraft with 4.5th-generation capabilities. The F-15EX Eagle II is as close to being a fifth-generation jet as any legacy airframe could be. The USAF first revealed the jet in 2021, and it only entered the inventory in 2024, but the F-15EX has nonetheless proven itself an impressive fighter. The USAF calls the F-15EX its missile truck due to its overwhelming number of loadouts. The aircraft is also fast, with a top speed of Mach 2.5 (1,918 mph), and it boasts two incredibly powerful Pratt & Whitney F100-PW-229 turbofan engines. These provide a combined thrust of 58,000 pounds, enabling the aircraft's incredible speed. While the F-15EX is rated for +9Gs, which is the standard limit for pilots, and not necessarily the aircraft, it can achieve up to 12Gs. Like other 12G-capable fighter jets, the F-15EX only pushes that limit during emergency situations. Fortunately, no pilots have fully blacked out while flying an F-15EX; some have come close during high-G operations. The flight computer has the capability to limit the Gs regardless of how much the pilot pulls on the stick, ensuring they remain conscious when they might otherwise push themselves beyond their limit. The 4.5th-generation fighter jet is an impressive machine, and it is strengthened for high Gs, but controlled by advanced software, ensuring pilot safety under extreme circumstances.

title: "I won't celebrate too early": GS's "Serve-ro" Kim Hyo-im, who clinched a 24-24 deuce, displays radiant humility: "I am just an assistant who helps out" [Jangchung on-site report] - 스타뉴스
content:
GS Caltex's second-year "Serve-ro (serve + libero)" Kim Hyo-im led her team to victory with a decisive serve that saved them from the brink of defeat. GS Caltex secured a 3-0 sweep victory over SOOP in the home game held at Jangchung Gymnasium in Jung-gu, Seoul on the 14th, in Round 1 of the women's division of the 'HK Huhguk Financial 2026~2027 V-League,' rising to second place in the league standings. The biggest turning point of the match was the first set. Kim Hyo-im, who entered as a substitute during a crisis where the team nearly lost the set, disrupted the opponent's reception with sharp serves. In a 25-24 set-point situation, she delivered a perfect service ace that pierced the far left corner of the court, putting an end to the tight deuce battle. After the game, Kim Hyo-im reflected, "The situation was extremely close, and we could have easily lost the set if we had made a mistake." She added, "I served with the mindset of 'let's just get it in and make one defensive play first.'" Regarding her final service ace, she explained, "On my first serve, I tried to aim for the sideline but it didn't go well, though fortunately it resulted in a point. After that, I found my rhythm and hit boldly, and it went in perfectly." The head coach also did not hold back his praise. Manager Lee Young-taek said, "We only had one substitution card available to strengthen serving and defense, which was Hyo-im, and she performed her role perfectly in the deuce situation," expressing satisfaction. He continued, "After returning from the national team, she has grown significantly enough to handle the libero position comfortably as well. Thanks to Hyo-im stepping up reliably, we were able to proceed boldly with (Yoo) Ga-ram's trade." Although she plays the specialized defensive position of libero, Kim Hyo-im primarily handles back-row defense and serving in the role of a "Serve-ro" due to the presence of starting libero Han Su-jin on the team. She grew further by wearing the national team badge during the off-season and competing in international tournaments such as the Asian Games. Kim Hyo-im shared, "Experiencing the power of overseas players broadened my defensive vision, and training with the senior players on the national team taught me a lot about my attitude toward volleyball." Although she joined team training after a short off-season, there was no sign of instability. Regarding her role within the team, she said, "I think of myself not as a mainstay, but as an 'assistant' who helps out. Rather than overthinking it, I am simply focused on being helpful to the team." Since joining last year, Kim Hyo-im has already experienced three titles in the V-League, the Asian Volleyball Confederation Cup, and the Yeosu Cup Tournament, earning her a reputation among fans as a player with so-called "winning luck." While stating, "I also believe I have winning luck," she expressed her determination: "I will not celebrate too early. I will not rest on my laurels or become complacent, but focus on winning one game at a time." <© STARNEWS. All rights reserved. title: Spurs 123-85 Warriors (Nov 13, 2026) Game Recap - ESPN
content: SAN ANTONIO -- — Stephon Castle scored a season-high 32 points, Victor Wembanyama had 12 points and 12 rebounds and the San Antonio Spurs won their 11th straight game, rolling past the Golden State Warriors 123-85 Friday night to remain unbeaten in NBA Cup play. Golden State's only double-figure scorers were L.J. Cryer with 20 points and Charles Bassey with 11. The Warriors are without Stephen Curry, who is sidelined at least two weeks with a right oblique tear suffered in a 115-108 loss in Houston on Wednesday. Golden State could have used a banner scoring night from the two-time MVP to overcome this lopsided loss. The Spurs led by 43 points in the third quarter, allowing the defending Western Conference champions to sit their starters and most of their key reserves for the entire fourth. Wembanyama was 5 for 11 from the field and 0 for 2 on 3-pointers while playing only 21 minutes and collecting his 121st career double-double. Warriors forward Draymond Green was issued a Flagrant Foul 1 for a forearm shove from behind off a running start that sent Wembanyama tumbling out of bounds with 6:47 remaining in the first half. Green, who exited and did not return in the first half after the Flagrant 1, finished with four points, three rebounds and three assists in 16 minutes. Golden State was 5 for 25 from the field in the opening quarter as San Antonio raced to a 38-14 lead. It was the fewest points scored in any quarter by a Spurs opponent this season, as well as a season low for the Warriors. Golden State trailed 63-33 at the half, the fewest points by a San Antonio opponent in the first half since Phoenix had 31 on Feb. 7, 2018. Castle shot 12 for 18 and was 5 for 8 on 3-pointers. He surpassed his previous high of 24 points against Oklahoma City on opening night on a slam dunk off an alley-oop pass on a finger roll from Wembanyama. title: How Will Higher-than-Expected Inflation Data Impact the Fed's Next Rate Decisions? - Goldman Sachs
content: We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. Goldman Sachs’ weekly newsletter, offering economic and markets analysis from across the firm. Subscribe now. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. While a smaller hike remains more likely, October’s hotter-than-expected inflation data may open the door to a 50-basis point rate hike at the Fed’s December meeting, says Muhammad Qubbaj, co-head of North America Interest Rate Product Sales and Trading in Goldman Sachs FICC and Equities. A recent drop in oil prices is unlikely to give the Fed cover to look past the CPI number without becoming more aggressive in the inflation fight, Qubbaj says on this episode of The Markets podcast. He also explains why his base case is for the 10-Year Treasury yield to remain below recent highs. Chris Hussey: This is The Markets. I'm Chris Hussey, and today is Thursday, November 12th, and we're here on the Goldman Sachs trading floor with Muhammad Qubbaj, who is co-head of North American Interest Rate Sales and Trading within FICC and Equities. And today, we're going to talk about how a hot CPI print this week is impacting rates and bonds markets, and how that has a carryover effect to other markets around the world. Chris Hussey: Okay, Q, let's start with the CPI print. It came in hot this week. What did you make of the market's reaction? How do you think the Fed is going to respond? Muhammad Qubbaj: Well, there's no rest for the wicked when you look at the sources of volatility in the market, whether it's geopolitics, whether it's the Fed, whether it's AI. We felt we almost had a little bit of a respite, maybe for five minutes, and all of a sudden CPI comes to the forefront and changes the board a little bit, too, and the Fed walks right back into the building. CPI affected us in three ways. First, I would say that it was unacceptable number, .3, third time in a row. Strong across all categories. The Fed has to reckon with that number, and the market priced that accordingly. Two, it wasn't just about the CPI level, it was about the Fed reaction function. We woke up that morning, Waller had made a speech and put 50s back on the table. He basically asked a question, and CPI answered. He said, "Contingent on .3, 50s could be on the table." And- Chris Hussey: And by 50s on the table, what you mean is that we could do a hike of 50 basis points, not 25. Muhammad Qubbaj: Exactly. So it just, again, underscored a hawkishness to the Fed and opened up the distribution to 50s, which was definitely a surprise that morning, before we even walked in and got the CPI number. The third thing was we spent almost a month executing a hike compression. We took out almost 50 basis points of hikes in the next one year, and some of this is a give back. So in terms of the market reaction, unwind of positioning and the high compression, a reaction to the strength of the CPI, the third one in a row and a re-understanding of the Fed's reaction function and opening up the distribution for 50s. Chris Hussey: All right, so it wasn't trivial. That's interesting. But you also talk about a Fed reaction function, and one of the things they have to react to is oil, I would imagine, because, this was an October report, but for the month of November, oil prices are now down 15%. How does oil factor into the rates market? Muhammad Qubbaj: We can't basically say that the causality between oil and rates is a one-for-one thing. They're definitely a participant. They definitely have a feed through to CPI, and they definitely show up into, basically, core CPI and how the Fed takes that number so that they can adjust policy. But, the sell-off wasn't just about oil when we had the big sell-off in the year. At one point it was about corporate earnings and growth. At another point it was a debate on the Fed reaction function uncertainty because they removed forward guidance term premium on the back of bond supply and CapEx supply, convexity hedging or the convexity profile of the market where we saw a lot of selling and positioning. Oil coming off in the last couple of weeks is definitely affects the level of rates, but you can't expect a full refund just based on the oil movement. Chris Hussey: Okay. Another thing that's changed since that October CPI print was the midterms. We got the midterms in early November. How does a change in Congress, if at all, have any impact on the rates market? Muhammad Qubbaj: I think a couple of things. One is the Fed's not a political body. It should not affect the Fed path, first order. It affects oil, obviously, based on the vote on the geopolitical outlook of the Iran war. Midterms affect oil, CPI affects the Fed. We've had almost triple the move based on the CPI morning print that we did in rates for the entire of midterms week. So I think that's where the focus is. Chris Hussey: Okay, Q, let's expand the conversation to 10-year bond yields. They have such an impact across markets. We were up at 5.3% not too long ago. They've come back to 5%. Are the conditions still in place, though, for us to eclipse the recent highs? Muhammad Qubbaj: You have to look at basically what took us to the peak in rates. There were several different factors. One, we had this new reaction function from the Fed, no forward guidance, the debate on how the Fed's reaction function will evolve under a Warsh leadership. You had the debate on term premium. You had the debate on Government issuance compounded by AI CapEx-related supply. You had a positioning situation in the market. You also had convexity selling in the market. All of those things contributed to the sell-off. So, I don't think that you're going to have that same set of circumstances reassert itself on the market again and push yields to the high, high level that we saw in October. Furthermore, you have two new breaks in the system: a Fed that is actively hiking, a hike lands in the front end but flattens the curve. Two, we had some sort of reflexivity that's been put onto the market in Warsh's last speech. He specifically tied the level of rates to the level of AI CapEx financing. So what happens when you do that is basically saying that you have a self-balancing system. If rates go up too much, then it can slow down the AI CapEx build-out, and it will almost have a self-balancing system from that perspective. But let us remember that if -- Do I think it's going to be a rate sell-off can happen again driven by positioning or term premium or supply worries or convexity selling? No. If we have a reassertion of strong earnings and I think that can give us some room. Chris Hussey: Yeah, a little bit of a growth-driven thing. Can I ask you to define one thing? Convexity selling, what is that? Muhammad Qubbaj: Convexity selling is a situation where, as the market sells off, people have more to sell. At its core, it means as things are getting worse, your flows are going to make it even worse. Chris Hussey: Right. It's a little technical factor. All right, let's talk about the competition between stocks, bonds, and credit. Cause that's always part of the equation here, I would imagine. How do you see that shaping up here? You talked about the growth equation being such a big one for where yields go from here. Muhammad Qubbaj: When we look at yields as it pertains to credit and as it pertains to equities, we have to look at it from a couple of lenses. What drives higher yields? Is it growth? Is it earnings? Then that should be good for the credit complex, and should be good for the equity complex. Is it driven by term premium worries and a supply absorption worries? Then you have a capital markets problem, and that's where they could be negative for equities, and it could be negative for credit. That's one factor. The other factor is the amount of leverage that we're talking about. When you're looking at a bond that is a corporation that is on the lower side of the spectrum of leverage, then higher rates affects the discount factor. When you look at a bond that's on the other side of the leverage spectrum, higher rates is a funding bill. It's a funding problem. So you can't... You have to be a little bit more nuanced when you say how do higher rates affect the equity market or credit market. It's a function of how did we get there, and how levered are the companies that we're talking about?  And that's basically where you get your answer. Chris Hussey: All right, lot to digest. Let's put a bow on it. What's the trade? Muhammad Qubbaj: I like to think of it from a serenity prayer perspective. Muhammad Qubbaj: Accept the things you cannot change. It is a one-factor market. It's all about mega-cap tech. Once you accept that, you realize that's the bet you're going to be making. Now, where do you have control? Where can you make some changes on the edges? One is how much of a size of a position you're going to take. It depends on how you hedge your portfolio. Two, the amount of leverage and what's the expression you take on mega cap to see basically how much exposure you have and how much factor risk you have. So we have discussed the risk. Now let's discuss the hedges. When you look at the hedges, you basically have out-of-the-money dollar puts. You have out-of-the-money equity puts. Delta one is favorable in the level of rates. A combination of those, you can build a carry neutral or positive carry hedge portfolio, and you can size it up and down depending on the amount of risk and leverage you're taking on the mega-cap tech. Now, you wanna own the factor, and you wanna rent the insurance. Chris Hussey: And by owning the factor, you want to own stocks. Chris Hussey: And by renting the insurance, you wanna maybe own some puts as well. Chris Hussey: All right, what are you looking for in the weeks ahead? Muhammad Qubbaj: Three sources of volatility we mentioned in the market. Oil, let's continue to see how the geopolitical, situation unfolds. The Fed, we are going to look at Fed speak and the Fed minutes and basically try to read the tea leaves and to see how hawkish the Fed is right now so we can get a feeling for the size. While, we're confident on the direction of which way the Fed is going. It's about size and timing right now. And the third factor is the AI economy. Anything, whether it's a capital market situation or an earning situation, anything that can continue to give us confidence or allow us to re-rate the level of risk in the market as it pertains to the AI economy. Chris Hussey: That's terrific. Q, you're always just a fountain of knowledge for us. Really appreciate you joining us. Chris Hussey: That does it for this week's episode of The Markets. I'm Chris Hussey. Thanks for listening. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels. GS Caltex uses Amazon SageMaker Canvas and Amazon SageMaker Pipelines to connect process engineers’ models to production workflows. The South Korean energy and chemical company divides model development and operations between engineers with complementary skills. Process engineers build and validate models in SageMaker Canvas without writing code, drawing on their process knowledge. Machine learning (ML) engineers configure SageMaker Pipelines workflows for deployment and scheduled inference. Moving assets from SageMaker Canvas into SageMaker Pipelines still required integration work. ML engineers had to set data paths for production, supply the model configuration, and connect preprocessing and inference jobs. GS Caltex automated this handoff while reusing the assets created in SageMaker Canvas. GS Caltex reports that its ML engineers now deploy models within a few hours, compared with about a week before. The company runs batch inference every 30 minutes, reducing the need for continuously running endpoints. GS Caltex reports that this has meaningfully lowered its inference costs. This post explains how GS Caltex connects SageMaker Canvas to SageMaker Pipelines and reuses validated preprocessing flows and models in production. The machine learning operations (MLOps) workflow has two paths: preparing a new model version for deployment, and running batch inference with the deployed model. You can use SageMaker Canvas to prepare data visually, build models, and generate batch predictions. You can also register validated models in Amazon SageMaker Model Registry from SageMaker Canvas. GS Caltex built a separate handoff process to turn these assets into executable SageMaker Pipelines steps. Process engineers understand the variables and data behind a process and assess whether a model’s predictions are useful. ML engineers turn the resulting assets into production jobs and manage model versions and execution history. The following diagram shows how process engineers hand off SageMaker Canvas assets to ML engineers for deployment and scheduled inference. ML engineers use Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) for preprocessing flows and Model Registry for model versions, then schedule pipeline runs through Amazon EventBridge. Figure 1: SageMaker Canvas assets connected to a SageMaker Pipelines workflow for scheduled batch inference ML engineers receive the preprocessing flow and model from SageMaker Canvas and review the data formats and prediction results. After that review, they approve the model in Model Registry and deploy it. This preparation takes place when a new model version is deployed. Subsequent inference runs reuse the deployed model. Amazon EventBridge starts each scheduled run. SageMaker Pipelines prepares the input data from Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), runs preprocessing and SageMaker Batch Transform, and stores the results in S3. ML engineers can inspect step status and Amazon CloudWatch logs to monitor the workflow. The production pipeline reuses the preprocessing logic and trained model created in SageMaker Canvas. ML engineers configure the input and output paths, set the order of execution, and write the code that connects approval and scheduling to the workflow. The full reference implementation is available in the GitHub repository. The code examples in this post focus on the connections between components. The repository uses a sample loan classification model, so adjust the configuration to match your model’s input and output formats. The following steps cover preprocessing reuse, model approval and deployment, pipeline construction, and scheduled inference. A preprocessing flow created with Data Wrangler in SageMaker Canvas records the data sources and transformation steps. To set up the reference implementation, export data to Amazon S3 using SageMaker Processing, then retrieve the job settings and the .flow file used by that job. In the export settings, turn off Auto job configuration and select SageMaker Processing. After the export starts, open the Processing job details on the Amazon SageMaker AI console. Record the container image URI, the S3 URI of the input named flow, the execution role, and the output settings. Use these values to configure the pipeline step that runs the .flow file. The SageMaker execution role must have permissions to read the required S3 data, write the results, and access the container image. Choose the instance type and count based on the volume of data you need to process. Keep the preprocessing logic validated by the process engineer, and adjust the data sources, paths, and other settings for the production environment. Check the container image and output node against the original job configuration. Some .flow files contain execution metadata such as internal_metadata.dw_job.container_uri. Check the actual Processing job settings rather than assuming that every export contains this field. If you move the workflow to another AWS Region, verify that the container image is available there. The reference implementation separates intermediate and final outputs by execution under runs/<execution-id>/. Its PrepareInput step writes data to a fixed S3 location referenced by the .flow file. Prevent executions that share that input path from overlapping. To isolate input data for each execution as well, add a preparation step that updates the source URI in a copy of the .flow file. Declaring a SageMaker Pipelines parameter does not automatically replace a URI inside the file. The target column is one difference between training and inference data. A flow built with training data can contain transformations that expect the target column in the input schema. Inference data does not contain that known outcome. The reference implementation adds a PrepareInput step before preprocessing. If the target column is missing, this step adds it with a placeholder value. After preprocessing, DropTargetColumn removes the column. Match the placeholder’s data type and column position to the training schema, and pass only the expected features to the model in their original order. Use this approach only when the placeholder target does not affect feature values. A flow that filters rows by the target, derives features from it, or applies target encoding needs additional treatment. In those cases, separate the transformations and learned state required for inference. Validation should cover column order and count, data types, missing-value handling, and row count. After removing the target, check that the remaining columns match the feature order used during training. Register the validated SageMaker Canvas model version in Model Registry. The registered version can include the model files, inference configuration, and evaluation results. ML engineers review this information before changing the approval status. The model file, such as model.tar.gz, must be used with the correct inference container and environment settings. A model package in Model Registry groups this information together. In this batch architecture, deployment creates a SageMaker model resource from an approved package for Batch Transform to reference. The following example checks a package that has already been approved, then creates the model resource. Supply model_package_arn, model_name, and sagemaker_role_arn during deployment. This example uses a unique model name for each version. Model Registry records approval status, but it does not enforce an approval check on every inference request. Check that status in the deployment code and retain the selected package ARN and model name in the pipeline configuration. If approval is revoked, update the schedules and execution configurations that use the model. Registration and deployment take place when a model version is released. The pipeline that runs every 30 minutes creates Batch Transform jobs using that model, so it does not need to register the model again on each run. Configure each job before connecting the steps. In the following example, prepare_args, preprocess_args, drop_target_args, and assemble_args hold the step arguments returned by run() calls on processors that use a PipelineSession. The processors and transformer share the pipeline_session object. Configure the transformer with the previously deployed model_name. The following execution graph shows the five steps in the sample loan model’s inference workflow. They prepare inputs, apply preprocessing, remove the target column, run batch inference, and assemble results. The execution was in the Executing state when this screenshot was taken. Figure 2: SageMaker Pipelines execution graph for the sample loan model Use depends_on to control execution order, and pass data through step output properties. For example, assemble_args must receive the location of the preprocessed data and predict.properties.TransformOutput.S3OutputPath. The output name "features" belongs to DropTargetColumn. The Data Wrangler step uses the output ID defined in its preprocessing flow. In the reference implementation, AssembleResults combines the preprocessed data and predictions by row position. Before using it in production, add checks that file order and row counts match, and stop result generation if they do not. If preprocessing sorts or removes rows, maintain an explicit mapping between source record IDs and predictions. GS Caltex runs inference every 30 minutes. The following example uses an Amazon EventBridge rule to schedule SageMaker Pipelines executions. Create the pipeline and verify it with a manual run before attaching the schedule. Set eventbridge_role_arn to a role that trusts the Amazon EventBridge service principal, events.amazonaws.com, and has sagemaker:StartPipelineExecution permission for the target pipeline. The pipeline_arn value identifies the pipeline created in the previous step. The expression rate(30 minutes) schedules runs at 30-minute intervals. To run on the hour and half hour, use cron(0/30 * * * ? *). Decide which data window each run processes in the input preparation step, and record it with the execution. Before enabling scheduled runs, check the total cost, execution time, and handling of invalid or mismatched data. Amazon SageMaker Pipelines is a serverless workflow orchestration service. It manages execution order and dependencies without a workflow server for you to provision or maintain. Processing and Batch Transform jobs use separate compute resources and are billed according to instance type and duration. A provisioned real-time endpoint is a good fit for requests that need a consistently low-latency response. Batch Transform suits workloads that can process a set of records together. It releases the job’s compute resources when the job finishes, so you can run predictions without keeping an inference endpoint running continuously for each model. A 30-minute schedule produces 48 scheduled runs per day. Include preprocessing, instance startup, inference, and postprocessing when estimating total runtime. The cost comparison should also account for Processing, S3, CloudWatch, and other services used by the workflow. Assess the cost of each workload using its measured usage, including the supporting services and the full runtime of every scheduled job. A schedule that starts a run every 30 minutes does not guarantee that each run finishes within that interval. Measure the full pipeline runtime with representative data, including instance startup and the time needed to retry failed jobs. Decide how to handle a scheduled run that arrives before the previous execution has finished. Controlling parallel steps within a pipeline does not prevent separate pipeline executions from overlapping. Check active executions, prevent duplicate processing of the same input window, and separate the output paths for each run. Record the input data window, preprocessing flow version, model package ARN, pipeline execution ARN, and output location for each run. These details help reproduce results and investigate errors. Complete the following checks before you enable the schedule: Add CloudWatch alerts for job failures and processing delays, together with data quality or model monitoring as needed. Set initial thresholds from measured runtime and data characteristics, and review them when the model or data volume changes. With a staged rollout, a team can verify the handoff before standardizing it across models. The following sections describe an adoption approach and the results GS Caltex reported. Start by validating the path to production for one model, then standardize the steps that repeat across deployments. The following sequence is a suggested adoption approach based on the GS Caltex experience. As automation expands, process engineers continue to assess whether the predictions are useful for the process. ML engineers manage pipeline execution and changes. GS Caltex reduced the repeated work needed to connect SageMaker Canvas models to production. ML engineers now deploy models within a few hours, compared with about a week previously. They also reuse the assets that process engineers validated in SageMaker Canvas. Process engineers began proposing applications in other processes after seeing their models used in production. ML engineers spent less time repeating integration work and could focus on operating and monitoring the pipelines. For a test deployment, disable the Amazon EventBridge rule and remove its targets first. After active pipeline executions and jobs have finished, delete the test pipeline and its SageMaker model resources. If you created a real-time endpoint for testing, delete it as well. Remove input, intermediate, and prediction files from S3, and clean up CloudWatch logs according to your retention policy. Check whether other executions or audit requirements still depend on model files and Model Registry versions before deleting them. At GS Caltex, process engineers create and validate models in SageMaker Canvas, and ML engineers use those assets to run production workflows in SageMaker Pipelines. This handoff reduced repeated integration work. GS Caltex reports that ML engineers now complete model deployments within a few hours, compared with about a week before. The handoff needs to include the preprocessing flow, input schema, inference configuration, and approval process alongside the model files. Verify that the workflow reproduces the expected results and can run reliably on the required schedule. To try this approach, start with one model you have validated in SageMaker Canvas and use the GitHub repository. See the SageMaker Pipelines developer guide for details on defining and running workflows. Check preprocessing and batch prediction results with a manual execution, then schedule runs at the interval your application needs. title: Why European Companies Are Forecast to Have Robust Earnings Growth - Goldman Sachs
content: We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. Goldman Sachs’ weekly newsletter, offering economic and markets analysis from across the firm. Subscribe now. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. European company earnings are growing rapidly—and at a faster pace than the euro area economy. The strong earnings have helped the stock market absorb higher bond yields, elevated energy prices, and subdued domestic economic growth, writes Sharon Bell, senior European equity strategist for Goldman Sachs Research, in a report. Our analysts expect earnings per share for the STOXX 600 index of European stocks to grow 18% in 2026 and 7% in 2027. Meanwhile, euro area nominal GDP is forecast to grow 3.3% in 2026 and 2.8% in 2027. “This raises an important question,” Bell writes. “Why are European earnings proving more resilient than the domestic economy would suggest?” Investors often use domestic GDP growth to gauge company earnings growth, Bell observes. “But this relationship is far from mechanical and can vary significantly over time,” she adds. For example, the two were roughly aligned in 2025 when euro area nominal GDP grew around 3.7% while STOXX 600 earnings growth was 2.4%. This year, though, earnings are expected to considerably outpace economic growth. (The STOXX 600 benchmark reflects a broader European footprint than the euro area, spanning companies domiciled in the UK, Switzerland, and Denmark, among others.) One possible reason why earnings of listed European companies appear to be decoupling from domestic economic growth could be the composition of sectors represented among Europe’s biggest stocks. “The equity market is a distorted mirror of the economy,” Bell writes. GDP measures value across the entire domestic economy, whereas aggregate market earnings reflect the profits of a concentrated group of large listed companies. For example, companies in the financial sector account for more than 30% of EURO STOXX earnings (an index of euro area stocks), but only 10% of euro area economic activity. Energy and technology are also more important to listed earnings, while real estate, retail, and industrials have much larger weights in the economy relative to the European stock market. Country exposure also helps to explain the divergence between European earnings and the domestic economy. Listed companies now generate most of their revenues outside their country of domicile, and the euro area’s share of STOXX 600 sales has fallen from more than 60% in 1990 to about one-third today. At the same time, exposure to the US, Asia, and emerging markets has increased steadily, Bell observes. “With more than half of STOXX 600 revenues now generated outside Europe, global rather than domestic growth is increasingly more relevant for listed companies.” Goldman Sachs Research captures this with sales-weighted GDP growth, which weights regional growth by the geographic breakdown of companies’ revenues in the prior year. This measure has exceeded euro area growth in most years since the early 2000s. It is also the dominant driver of earnings: A 1 percentage point acceleration is associated with roughly 10 percentage points of higher STOXX 600 EPS growth. Currency also matters. A weaker euro raises the translated value of overseas profits, a meaningful share of which is denominated in US dollars, and improves the competitiveness of European companies. Europe is a net energy importer, so higher prices squeeze households and raise corporate costs. But the economy's sensitivity to oil prices has declined as the euro area economy has become less dependent on oil. The market's composition also provides a cushion: companies involved in energy and basic resources benefit directly from higher commodity prices, while chemicals companies and many industrial companies can pass costs on to customers. The cushion may not last. Sustained high energy costs can weaken company profit margins as growth and pricing power fade. The negative impact of higher costs can take time to appear in margins: After the 2022 energy shock, earnings for energy companies rose quickly while easing supply bottlenecks supported autos and chemicals companies; six to 12 months later, earnings estimates for energy and chemicals companies began to fall as commodity prices normalized and cost pressure became more visible. The current Middle East shock could follow a similar sequence, with margins outside financials and commodities coming under pressure if demand slows and pricing power fades. Given that our economists do not expect significant changes in euro area economic growth momentum, Bell’s team is more cautious than the consensus of financial analysts when it comes to European companies’ profit margins. Goldman Sachs Research forecasts broadly flat margins for STOXX 600 companies until 2028 after financials and commodities are excluded. On the other hand, the consensus of analysts expects margins to expand by more than 100 basis points to 10.1% from 8.7%. title: The Global Economy Is Forecast to Grow 2.8% in 2027 as Oil Prices Decline - Goldman Sachs
content: We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. Goldman Sachs’ weekly newsletter, offering economic and markets analysis from across the firm. Subscribe now. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. Goldman Sachs Research expects steady global economic growth in 2027, as lower energy prices and still-strong capital expenditures in artificial intelligence (AI) outweigh tighter financial conditions and more neutral fiscal policy. Global GDP is predicted to increase 2.8% in 2027, up from 2.7% this year, Jan Hatzius, chief economist and head of Goldman Sachs Research, writes in a report. The economies of the US, Japan, and the UK are among those projected to grow faster than the consensus of economist estimates. As has been the case for the last several years, our economists are more optimistic than consensus on US economic expansion owing to resilient investment. They are more downbeat on the European growth outlook amid tighter financial conditions and their expectation that higher energy prices will start to bite this winter. Goldman Sachs Research also forecasts continued robust economic expansion in South Korea and Taiwan, reflecting another year of strong AI exports. While growth is expected to be solid, the risks to Goldman Sachs Research’s forecast for global GDP growth “are tilted to the downside,” Hatzius writes. Renewed escalation in the Iran war could result in another energy price surge. Large fiscal deficits could push up long-term yields more sharply, especially in France. AI capex could be lower than expected because of capacity constraints, regulation, credit market stress, or weaker demand, and Hatzius also sees early signs that AI adoption is weighing on the job market. “We expect another year of solid but unremarkable GDP growth in 2027, but several of the impulses that shaped global growth in 2026 will look different,” Hatzius writes. How will oil and energy prices affect GDP growth in 2027? The headwind from the energy supply shock will likely flip next year as energy prices normalize. The baseline forecast from Goldman Sachs Research’s commodity strategists is that continued Middle East supply adaptation will lower Brent prices to $78 per barrel by the end of 2027, with a similar normalization in global prices for liquefied natural gas. At the same time, Goldman Sachs Research sees an ongoing drag from energy prices in Europe from delayed energy cost pass-through to consumers. How financial conditions and the fiscal outlook will affect GDP growth Lower energy prices should outweigh the effect of tighter financial conditions and a smaller fiscal impulse to GDP expansion in 2027, Hatzius writes. Goldman Sachs Research’s Financial Conditions Index implies a moderate drag on growth over the next few quarters. While our economists do not “expect meaningful fiscal consolidation” in 2027, the large fiscal expansions of the last few years are fading. The main exception is in Japan, where consumption tax cuts, increased defense spending, and the government’s investment plans are forecast to boost GDP growth by 0.7 percentage point. “We also expect modestly positive impulses in Germany and the US—where the Democratic victory in November’s US election suggests some of the spending cuts from the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act will be reversed,” Hatzius writes. Our economists project a continued fiscal drag in the UK that leaves the fiscal impulse in developed markets “only slightly positive.” Goldman Sachs Research expects AI capex to boost global economic growth again next year. Our analysts forecast that nominal global AI investment will rise to $1.8 trillion in 2027 from $1.1 trillion this year, mostly driven by an increase of over $500 billion in hardware spending in the US. The investment surge is projected to be frontloaded, with the year-over-year change in investment as a share of GDP peaking in the first half of 2027. “Even with the expected slowdown, the impact on GDP growth will be sizable,” Hatzius writes. Our economists estimate that AI investment will boost GDP growth by 0.4 percentage point globally. In the US, Goldman Sachs Research estimates AI investment will give a 0.6-percentage-point boost to "true" GDP growth after accounting for continued undercounting of semiconductor investment and chip-related intellectual property exports. The transition to an AI-enabled economy, meanwhile, is occurring in two phases, according to Goldman Sachs Research. The first phase involves an investment boom that raises both corporate profits and global GDP growth but features only limited productivity gains. The second phase involves less hardware investment but more business reorganization, as well as more substantial productivity gains and labor market disruption. Goldman Sachs Research has argued that AI is likely to displace some jobs and cause a temporary increase in the unemployment rate. Our economists’ baseline expectation is that AI adoption will only have a small effect on the labor market in 2027 and there will be more notable effects in 2028-2029. What is the outlook for China’s economic growth in 2027? Goldman Sachs Research forecasts China’s GDP to grow 4.5% in 2027, compared with the consensus estimate of 4.4%. This “reflects very robust expectations for Chinese exports and a further increase in China’s trade surplus,” Hatzius writes. By contrast, domestic demand growth is predicted to remain weak next year owing to a drag from the property sector and weak underlying consumer spending. This is expected to result in a modest headwind of 0.1 percentage point to the rest of the world’s GDP growth, with larger drags on growth in manufacturing-heavy economies such as Germany (headwind of 0.3 percentage point) and Central Europe (headwind of 0.2 percentage point). Under Goldman Sachs Research’s baseline commodity forecasts for a steady decline in energy prices next year, inflation should slow in 2027, Hatzius writes. The case for disinflation is particularly strong in the US because the price boosts from tariffs should fully drop out of the year-over-year inflation statistics next spring, he writes. With tariff effects fading and a much smaller inflation boost from the war in Iran, our economists expect core PCE inflation to slow to 2.4% at the end of 2027 from 3.2% at the end of 2026. “We forecast a steady decline in year-over-year core inflation in the US and a more delayed decline in other major economies once the energy price shock is fully digested,” Hatzius writes. What is the outlook for the Fed and other central banks in 2027? Goldman Sachs Research expects “incremental policy tightening” through early 2027 in most major economies, but its economic forecasts support a dovish view on rates next year. Central banks could either deliver gradual normalization cuts later in 2027 as inflation comes down, or they could pivot to cuts sooner if economic growth is slower than projected. The US Federal Reserve is expected to hike rates in December and March in response to lingering inflation pressures. But our economists say softer inflation data should allow the Fed to cut once in December 2027, followed by three more cuts in 2028 to a terminal rate of 3.25-3.5%. “Furthermore, we see more dovish rate risks in the US than in most other economies, both because US inflation drivers look more clearly temporary and because the US is most exposed to a downturn in the AI cycle,” Hatzius writes. Our economists’ views on other major developed markets also skew dovish. The European Central Bank is forecast to deliver its final hike in December, before starting to normalize back toward a 2.25% terminal rate in the fourth quarter of 2027. Goldman Sachs Research expects a final hike from the Bank of England to 4.25% in February before a hold for the remainder of 2027. Our economists forecast normalization cuts from the BoE to a 3.25% terminal rate, but not until 2028. “The main outlier to our forecast of only modest further policy tightening is Japan,” Hatzius writes. Goldman Sachs Research expects the Bank of Japan to hike rates by 25 basis points in December, reflecting recent communication from the central bank highlighting both upside inflation risks and the impact of higher global interest rates on the Japanese yen. With core CPI (excluding fresh food but including energy) likely to rise above 3.5% through next summer, our economists now expect that the BoJ will follow through with additional hikes in March and June for a terminal rate of 2%. title: This Christmas, remember your local stores! - Statesboro Herald

With Christmas fast approaching, now is the time to think about what you're buying and where you're buying it. Online shopping has certainly changed the way we shop, but don't overlook the many locally owned stores right here in Statesboro. You might be surprised at how competitive their prices are! At McKeithen's Hardware, we'll match the regular price of any locally available item that's in stock at a competing retailer. Just ask! Shopping locally also gives you something you can't get from a picture on a computer screen: the opportunity to see what you're buying, ask questions and get advice before you make a purchase. After all, the most expensive product is the one you buy that doesn't do the job! And there's another good reason to shop local. Some combine Latin pop with dancehall rhythms. Others create dreamy alternative R&B or use electronic production to make melancholy songs feel suitable for a club. “BbY WOW” is particularly interesting because it combines those approaches. Featuring The Weeknd, “LA FAMA” combines Latin rhythmic influences with atmospheric R&B vocals. It’s less obviously dancehall-oriented than “BbY WOW”. title: 2026 Global Alternatives Survey: The LP View - Goldman Sachs Asset Management
content:
Despite geopolitical uncertainty, inflation concerns and liquidity constraints, institutional investors remain committed to private markets. Most respondents view opportunities across private equity, private credit and infrastructure as equal to or better than last year, and more than a third expect to deploy more capital. As a result, investors are not retreating from private markets, but becoming more selective in how they allocate capital, manage liquidity and choose investment managers. Many remain under allocated to private markets, particularly private credit and infrastructure, suggesting continued room for capital deployment. While slower distributions continue to constrain new commitments, investor appetite remains resilient. In response, investors are placing greater emphasis on liquidity management, with secondaries and co-investments becoming increasingly important components of portfolio construction. Manager quality remains a key driver of capital allocation decisions, with investors increasingly focused on underwriting discipline, specialist expertise and differentiated investment approaches. At the same time, respondents identified artificial intelligence as the leading force expected to reshape the private markets industry over the next five years. Together, these trends suggest investors are raising the bar for manager selection, seeking firms with both proven investment capabilities and the ability to adapt to structural changes across private markets. For the third consecutive year, geopolitics ranks as the leading investment risk. Geopolitical tensions were ranked among the top five risks by 82% of respondents, followed by inflation at 67% and the risk of an economic slowdown or recession in the US at 63%. More than a third of respondents, 37%, expect to deploy more capital than last year, while 47% plan to maintain their current pace. Lack of distributions is the most frequently cited factor affecting deployment plans. AI is expected to be the leading driver of change in the alternatives industry over the next five years, ranking ahead of industry consolidation and economic disruption. As adoption becomes more commonplace, attention is shifting toward identifying managers that can use AI to enhance investment decisions, create value across portfolio companies, and generate differentiated outcomes.
